sentences.text: Taurovenator is classified as a very large carcharodontosaurid within the family Carcharodontosauridae.
It ranks among the largest known theropod dinosaurs and stands as one of the biggest terrestrial carnivores.
Comparisons with related species estimate the skull of this predator to be around 135 cm long.
A defining trait is a postorbital bone that projected outward like a horn, measuring 3-4 cm in height and 2-3 cm in diameter.
The neck vertebrae featured prominent neural spines with flange-like dorsal tips, forming an interlocking structure resembling overlapping roof tiles.
One known dorsal vertebra possessed a neural arch that was 52 cm high.

Despite its massive size, the orbital horn is relatively robust but small and rounded, clearly disconnected from the edge, while an orbital section length of 12 centimeters suggests it is considered a medium-sized theropod based on that specific measurement.
The outward-projecting horn on the postorbital bone is a trait distinct from other carcharodontosaurids.
Researchers described the unique interlocking neck vertebrae as a 'cervical complex' that resembles overlapping roof tiles.
The genus Taurovenator was named by Motta and colleagues in 2016, establishing the group formally.
The type species of this genus is Taurovenator violantei.
Initially, the animal was known only from a single right postorbital bone unearthed by Matias Motta in 2005 from the lower member of the Huincul Formation.
This fossil was found on Violante Farm at Rancho Violante, located on the shores of Lake Ezequiel Ramos Mexía in Rio Negro Province, Argentina.
In 2024, a previously undescribed partial skeleton found at the same site was referred to Taurovenator.
Fossilized pollen from the Huincul Formation indicates a diverse plant community including ferns, gymnosperms, and angiosperms.
Motta et al. (2016) classified Taurovenator as a derived member of Carcharodontosauridae, closely related to Giganotosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, and Mapusaurus.
The parent group for Taurovenator is Carcharodontosauridae.
Taurovenator fossils were found in the Huincul Formation, which consists of yellowish and greenish fine-to-medium grain sandstones, some containing volcanic ash.
The environment where Taurovenator lived was a braided river drainage system.
Taurovenator lived in the middle Cretaceous, approximately 96 to 91 million years ago, in what is now South America.
The age of Taurovenator's deposits was previously estimated to be between the Cenomanian and Turonian, or possibly the Early Turonian to Late Santonian.
The Paleobi Database records the time range of Taurovenator as the Albian, between 110.1 and 106.3 million years ago.
Some paleontologists have debated whether Taurovenator is synonymous with the genus Mapusaurus.
Coria et al. (2019) suggested Taurovenator is synonymous with Mapusaurus because their original distinguishing features were shared, arguing that its unique features were shared with Mapusaurus.
Researcher Mickey Mortimer believed Taurovenator was synonymous with Mapusaurus due to insufficient diagnostic material.
Differences in stratigraphic layers suggest Taurovenator, Meraxes, and Mapusaurus may not have lived at the same time, supporting Taurovenator's validity.
A 2025 study by Cau and Paterna debated the classification of Taurovenator, placing it outside the family Carcharodontosauridae.
